channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Australian house prices fell for a fifth straight month in August, though the two main indices disagree on the size: Cotality recorded a 0.9% monthly fall and 3.6% below the March peak, while REA Group recorded 0.2% and 2.7% peak to trough.
item.description:
The two data providers agree on direction and duration but not on magnitude, and both figures are worth carrying rather than choosing between them. Cotality's national home value index fell 0.9% month-on-month in August, putting values 3.6% below the March 2026 peak, with 93% of capital city suburbs declining through winter, quarterly sales 15.5% lower than a year earlier and advertised capital city listings 24% higher year-on-year as homes take longer to sell. REA Group put the August fall at 0.2% and the peak-to-trough decline at 2.7%, noting prices remain 1.8% higher than a year ago. Cotality expects further falls, citing persistently low new housing supply, negative real wage growth and the possibility of another rate rise. That last point has support: ANZ now expects the Reserve Bank of Australia to raise rates by 25 basis points to 4.60% in November, and consumer confidence fell 2.6 points to 74.9 last week with four-week inflation expectations at 5.9%.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Residential construction and renovation are meaningful end-markets for adhesive technologies, and a fifth consecutive monthly decline with lengthening selling times points to softer renovation activity ahead of any change in new-build volumes. Cotality lists persistently low new housing supply alongside negative real wage growth and a possible rate rise among the reasons falls are expected to continue; the sources do not separate supply from demand effects on construction volumes. An expected November rate rise would tighten conditions further. Points that may be worth considering include whether Australian construction demand assumptions distinguish between the renovation and new-build channels, given that these are moving for different reasons.

MarketScreener | Herald Sun | ABC | MarketScreener

item.title: China's state planning agency again warned against "blindly following the trend and rushing in all at once" in robotics, echoing earlier warnings about repetitive products and squeezed research budgets, as AI-driven listings raised about USD 54 billion.
item.description:
The commission made the remark at a regular press conference, and it is a repetition rather than a new position: an official warned in August 2025 against blind trend-following in emerging fields, and at the end of last year the commission noted that as humanoid robot companies multiplied there was a need to guard against the market being flooded with highly repetitive products and against research budgets being squeezed. Reporting places the warnings against the experience of new energy vehicles, lithium batteries and photovoltaics, where low-level duplicate capacity and price competition followed rapid entry. The market is moving the other way for now. Fortune puts this year's Chinese IPO proceeds at about USD 54 billion, with S&P Global Market Intelligence attributing the boom to investor appetite for AI and robotics; memory chipmaker CXMT raised more than USD 8.6 billion in Shanghai in July with shares up 466% on debut, and Unitree's August listing rose about 460% on its first day. Industrial robot production rose 28.5% year-on-year in the seven months to July to 635,000 units, and China's robot rental market, above CNY 1 billion in 2025, is projected by iiMedia Research to exceed CNY 10 billion in 2026 — a projection, not an outcome. A separate index from OpenMind scores China at 95 and the United States at 48.5 on materials and supply chain for robotics, estimating that building a humanoid robot without Chinese suppliers would cost around USD 131,000 against about USD 46,000.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Robotics has been reported here mostly as expansion, so a regulator repeatedly cautioning against overcapacity in the same sector is a useful counterweight. If the pattern the commission names does repeat, the sequence seen in photovoltaics and lithium batteries — rapid capacity build, price competition, consolidation — would affect suppliers of assembly adhesives and coatings through both volume and pricing, and would change which customers survive to place repeat orders. The supply-chain concentration figures are a separate matter: on OpenMind's scoring, building without Chinese suppliers roughly triples component cost, which may weigh on where assembly is located. Points that may be worth considering include how robotics-sector customer exposure is weighted between volume growth and consolidation risk.

Beijing Daily | Fortune | AP | China Economic Net | Forbes

item.title: Chief US District Judge Brenda Sannes ruled that New York cannot enforce its 2024 Climate Change Superfund Act, which sought USD 75 billion from fossil fuel companies over 25 years, finding it pre-empted by the federal Clean Air Act.
item.description:
The ruling on 31 August sided with 22 Republican state attorneys general and industry groups including the US Chamber of Commerce. Judge Sannes found that the Clean Air Act, which gives the federal Environmental Protection Agency authority to regulate carbon dioxide emissions, does not authorise states to adopt emissions compensation schemes of this kind. She wrote that enforcing the act risked upsetting the balance between preventing global warming — a project she described as requiring national standards and global participation — and promoting economic growth, energy production, foreign policy interests and national security. The decision concerns a state statute and federal pre-emption; it is a district-court ruling and reporting does not indicate whether an appeal will follow.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The direct subject is fossil fuel producers, but the reasoning is what carries wider relevance: a finding that federal emissions authority pre-empts state-level retrospective cost recovery narrows one route by which US states have sought to assign historical climate costs to industry. The decision concerns New York's statute alone, and reporting does not address whether it will be read across to comparable measures elsewhere; a single district court ruling is also not settled law, and appeals commonly follow. For chemical manufacturers the read-across is indirect and concerns the general contours of climate liability exposure in the US rather than any immediate obligation. Points that may be worth considering include whether US climate-liability scenarios in risk registers reflect a federal pre-emption argument, and how this sits against the opposite regulatory direction in the EU.

MarketScreener

item.title: From 27 September the EU's EmpCo Directive applies stricter requirements to environmental marketing claims on labelling and imagery, allowing terms such as "eco-friendly", "sustainable" or "climate-neutral" only with recognised, verifiable evidence.
item.description:
The directive reaches product labelling and product imagery, not only written claims. General environmental claims are permitted only where they can be substantiated by recognised and verifiable evidence, which removes the option of unqualified descriptors used without a supporting basis. European Coatings reports that paint and coatings manufacturers must ensure their environmental claims and sustainability-related product communications comply, The source addresses coatings specifically, though the requirements are drafted around consumer-facing environmental claims generally. The date is close: 27 September falls under four weeks from now, and because the directive reaches imagery as well as wording, the affected material is likely to extend beyond the label itself.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is a communications and documentation requirement rather than a technical one, which makes it unusual among current EU chemical rules and changes where the work sits internally. The affected material is likely to be distributed across marketing, regulatory and packaging functions, and artwork change cycles may not accommodate the remaining window. Substantiation is the operative test: a claim that can be evidenced to a recognised standard remains usable, while one resting on internal assessment alone may not. Points that may be worth considering include which existing claims across EU-facing labels and collateral currently rest on recognised third-party evidence, and whether artwork change cycles allow revisions before the date.

European Coatings

item.title: Germany's preliminary August inflation rate reached 2.9%, matching April and the highest since a 3.7% reading in December 2023, driven by higher prices for fuels and heating oil, with one bank analyst expecting it to climb above 3% in the autumn.
item.description:
The Federal Statistical Office's preliminary figure puts August inflation at 2.9%, the same level as April. Silke Tober of the Hans Böckler Foundation's IMK institute attributed the increase to fuels and heating oil rather than to broader price pressure, which points back to the energy shock rather than to domestic demand. Elmar Völker of LBBW said inflation could rise above 3% again in the autumn — a forecast from one analyst, not a consensus. The reading arrives ahead of the European Central Bank's rate decision on 10 September. Other German data released alongside it pointed in different directions. Foreign direct investment into Germany rose about 50% in 2025 to roughly EUR 86 billion, on German Economic Institute (IW) calculations using Bundesbank transaction data, with UK inflows quadrupling to more than EUR 26 billion and overtaking the United States, while US investment fell nearly 44% to EUR 11.8 billion and its share of the total dropped to about 14% from more than 36%. Real GDP grew 0.4% in the first quarter and 0.3% in the second. The chemical association VCI criticised government legislation it says slows industrial value creation, warning that Germany's leading position in the healthcare industry risks becoming a pure sales market for international competitors.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

An inflation reading driven by fuels and heating oil rather than by wages or services has a particular character for energy-intensive manufacturing: it raises operating costs directly while giving the central bank less reason to read it as entrenched. That combination can leave producers absorbing higher energy bills without an offsetting easing in financing costs. The foreign investment figures cut the other way and are a genuine positive, though the shift in composition away from US capital toward UK capital is itself a change worth noting. Points that may be worth considering include how energy-cost assumptions for the autumn are framed if inflation moves above 3%, and how the VCI's regulatory concerns intersect with production-location reviews.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | MarketScreener | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | China Daily | Politico Europe

item.title: The Bloomberg Agriculture Spot Index rose more than 13% during August, likely its largest monthly gain since July 2012, with wheat one of the main drivers after attacks on Black Sea ports and ships cut Russian and Ukrainian exports.
item.description:
The immediate driver is the Black Sea rather than the Middle East. Recent attacks by Russia and Ukraine on each other's ports and shipping sharply reduced exports from both countries' main wheat-producing regions, pushing wheat to three-year highs; together the two account for more than a quarter of global wheat exports and are also major suppliers of barley, corn and sunflower oil. Other exporters have struggled to fill the gap, unsold grain is accumulating, and Ukraine's agriculture ministry expects farmers to reduce winter wheat plantings for 2027, which would extend the effect beyond this season. A second and slower factor is building separately: an El Niño event, possibly the strongest on record, is still developing, and a Bloomberg Economics study calculates that the resulting drought has coincided with a rise of almost two percentage points in consumer prices in the Philippines and Indonesia. Farmers facing these conditions are also absorbing higher diesel and fertiliser costs arising from the US-Iran conflict, so the pressures compound.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Agricultural commodity prices reach adhesive technologies along two routes. The first is bio-based feedstocks, where starch, vegetable-oil and other crop-derived inputs used in some adhesive technologies chemistries become more expensive and less predictable when grain and oilseed markets move this far in a month. The second is demand: food and beverage producers are among the largest buyers of packaging adhesives, and input-cost pressure of this scale tends to show up in packaging specification and volume decisions. The Ukrainian planting forecast and the developing El Niño both suggest the pressure may persist past this harvest rather than resolve with it. Points that may be worth considering include the degree of bio-based feedstock exposure in current formulations, and whether food and beverage customers are signalling changes to packaging plans.

Lianhe Zaobao | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met for the second time this year at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, pledging deeper trade, energy and technology cooperation, alongside Iran's president and India's prime minister.
item.description:
The summit brought Xi, Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi to Bishkek alongside Central Asian leaders, Pakistan and Belarus. Xi and Putin reiterated deepening strategic coordination and named trade, energy, technology and multilateral mechanisms as areas for closer work, with Putin adding industry, transport and science; Putin said the two countries are implementing major energy, industrial, space, transport and logistics projects and that mutual agricultural shipments grew 34%, and raised the possibility of normalising a visa-free arrangement. Xi framed the meeting in terms of promoting a multipolar world and global governance reform. In bilateral meetings Xi urged Kyrgyzstan to deepen practical cooperation, diversify traded products and expand law-enforcement and security cooperation, with the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway described as progressing steadily; with Uzbekistan he named artificial intelligence and anti-desertification alongside the same railway; and with Mongolia he raised green minerals, artificial intelligence and the digital economy in addition to established trade and energy links. Modi met Putin and said it was time to move "from endless war to the end of war", with talks covering energy, defence, innovation, space, fertilisers and people-to-people links. Separately, at the G20 finance meeting in Asheville, Bessent told Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov that no economic relief is possible until the war in Ukraine ends.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The summit's substance for industry lies less in the communiqués than in the specific corridors named. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is named in both the Kyrgyz and Uzbek bilaterals; reporting does not describe its routing, so any read-across to China-Europe freight alternatives is inference rather than established fact. The green-minerals thread in the Mongolia discussion touches input chains for electronics and magnets. Set against that, Bessent's message to Moscow signals no near-term easing of the sanctions environment. Points that may be worth considering include whether Central Asian overland capacity is worth monitoring as a hedge in freight planning, and how a widening China-Russia industrial relationship interacts with European compliance obligations.

Commercial Times | Commercial Times | Interfax | Lianhe Zaobao | Chinatimes | Xinhua | Xinhua | China Daily | Global Times | The Times of India | The Guardian

item.title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he believes Japan's government and central bank will act to strengthen the yen, telling CNBC he has information the market does not; the yen firmed to about 159.81 and odds of a September rise reached 73%.
item.description:
Bessent met Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda, and said he expects Ueda to "do the right thing" on monetary policy to counter the yen's decline. The remark that he holds information the market does not is an unusually explicit intervention by a US Treasury Secretary in commentary on another country's central bank, and the currency responded: the yen had weakened past 160 per dollar in the two preceding sessions and firmed to about 159.81, with markets pricing a 73% chance of a rise later in September. Analysts quoted said the move would need stronger follow-through from the central bank to hold. The domestic data pointed the same way. Capital spending rose 1.6% year-on-year in the June quarter and 1.5% on a seasonally adjusted quarterly basis, with recurring profits up 24.6% to a record JPY 44.7 trillion and sales up 5.9%; one economist attributed the investment pressure to global AI competition. Those figures feed the revised GDP release due on 8 September, against a preliminary reading of 1.1% annualised growth, down from 1.9%. The Nikkei 225 fell 1.97% to 65,096.63. Teikoku Databank counted 4,923 food and beverage items scheduled for price rises in September, the largest monthly wave in over three years, attributing it partly to higher crude and naphtha prices raising packaging-material costs, alongside labour, logistics and import costs.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The packaging link in the Japanese price data is the most directly relevant point: Teikoku Databank names crude and naphtha costs feeding into packaging materials as one driver of the September increases, which is the same input chain that reaches adhesives and coatings. A stronger yen would cut Japanese importers' input costs while making Japanese exports less competitive, so the direction of benefit depends on where value is added. Capital spending up 1.6% with record profits suggests Japanese industrial customers retain capacity to invest. Points that may be worth considering include how currency assumptions for the fourth quarter are set given an explicit US push for yen appreciation, and whether packaging-linked demand in Japan softens as those price rises reach shelves.

Channel News Asia | The Straits Times | The Economic Times | MarketScreener | The Mainichi | The Economic Times | Japan Today

item.title: Trump told Canadian companies to move their headquarters and production to the US, calling Canada "one of the worst abusers", as analysts identified Toyota and Honda as the most exposed to the planned 50% tariff on Canadian-built vehicles.
item.description:
Trump's posts on 30 August urged Canadian firms doing business with the United States to relocate headquarters and production, said companies were already returning, and put the annual US trade loss with Canada at more than USD 60 billion. No specific companies planning relocations were named in reporting, and the scale of any investment moving across the border was not established. The tariff sequence is now clearer than it was a week ago: the US imposed 50% duties on almost USD 20 billion of Canadian imports on 22 August, Canada's counter-tariffs of 15%, 25% and 50% on CAD 27.6 billion of US imports take effect on 8 September and cover steel, dairy, plywood and household paper products among others, and the threatened 50% tariff on Canadian-built vehicles is scheduled for 1 January 2027, doubling the present 25%. The analytical addition is who carries that last one: Toyota and Honda together account for more than 75% of Canada's vehicle production, and analysts warn the increase could force them to close some assembly lines, with a trade agreement still able to avert it. The Canadian dollar weakened to a nine-day low of about 1.39 per US dollar, which reporting attributes to Bank of Canada expectations and hawkish Fed comments rather than to the tariffs directly. Ottawa announced more than CAD 12.5 million of repayable investment for nine affected businesses in the Hamilton area. One US analysis put the raw-material cost increase for toilet paper at up to 11% and for paper towels at up to 31%.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Two exposures are worth separating. The automotive one is dated and quantified: a January 2027 step from 25% to 50% concentrated on two manufacturers that make most of Canada's vehicles, which would reach adhesive technologies suppliers through assembly-line volumes rather than through the tariff itself. The pulp, paper and packaging one is nearer, since Canada's 8 September list covers household paper and a range of pulp and paper products, and the estimated raw-material increases of up to 11% for toilet paper and up to 31% for paper towels point to cost pressure across pulp- and paper-based inputs, though those estimates cover tissue rather than packaging grades. The relocation appeals are so far statements without documented moves, which may make actual relocation announcements a more informative signal than the rhetoric. Points that may be worth considering include how much North American footprint planning should respond to a tariff that remains negotiable, and whether packaging customers have visibility of their September input costs.

The Independent | The Economic Times | Daily Times | The Nation | Commercial Times | Anadolu Agency | The Boston Globe | Business Recorder | CBC | The Daily Mail

item.title: India's GDP rose 7.8% year-on-year in the June quarter, above the Reserve Bank of India's 7% forecast and market expectations of about 7.2%, up from a revised 6.9% a year earlier but down from 8.6% in the January-March quarter.
item.description:
The comparison chosen changes the story, so both are worth stating. Against the same quarter a year earlier, growth accelerated from a revised 6.9%; against the immediately preceding quarter, it slowed from 8.6%. Either way the figure exceeded the Reserve Bank's own 7% forecast and market expectations of about 7.2%,. Gross value added grew 8.2% and nominal GDP 10.3%. By sector, manufacturing grew 9.2% against 8.3% a year earlier, financial services 12.1% against 8.8%, construction 7.7%, electricity and utilities 8.9%, and agriculture 3.6%, while mining contracted 2.4%. Credit growth reached 18.3%, described as the highest in over a decade. The context is an economy that imports about 90% of its oil, more than half of which came from the Middle East before the war. Prime Minister Modi called the result a "herculean feat" Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman credited the people and government reforms, and Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran attributed part of the resilience to keeping critical inputs available through the crisis. The opposition Congress party disputed the reading, arguing that the number does not reflect depressed private investment sentiment, sluggish consumer confidence, falling household savings and record household debt. Separately, July industrial production growth slowed to 6.7% from 8.8% in June.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

For manufacturers serving India, the composition matters more than the headline. Construction at 7.7% and manufacturing at 9.2% are the segments that drive demand for adhesive technologies; manufacturing outgrew the 7.8% headline rate while construction ran marginally below it, and the 2.4% contraction in mining and the slower July industrial production print are cautions against reading the quarter as uniformly strong. The 18.3% credit growth suggests customers have been able to finance activity, though rising domestic yields may make that harder to sustain. Points that may be worth considering include whether India's resilience through an energy shock changes its weight in regional capacity planning, and how much of the growth reflects underlying demand rather than the front-loading of activity ahead of higher input costs.

The Hindu Business Line | The Hindu Business Line | The Financial Times | Il Sole 24 Ore | Business Standard | The Economic Times | The Times of India | LiveMint | Forbes India

item.title: The US 10-year Treasury yield passed 4.75% for the first time since January 2025, France's 10-year reached about 4.17%, its highest since the 2008 financial crisis, and India's benchmark yield hit its highest level since June.
item.description:
Three markets moved for overlapping but distinct reasons. In the United States, the 10-year yield passed 4.75% for the first time since 14 January 2025 and the 30-year rose about four basis points to 5.248%, with five-year yields at their highest since early 2025; the move was driven by the oil price and by expectations that the Federal Reserve may raise rates. Market-implied odds of a September increase are now put at between 57% and 60% depending on the source; the CME FedWatch reading of nearly 60% is up from 41.4% a week earlier. President Trump said it would be "absurd" to raise rates while adding that he respects Fed chair Kevin Warsh and expects him to do what he has to do. In France, the 10-year rose almost five basis points to nearly 4.17%, a high since the 2008 crisis, on fiscal and political grounds rather than energy: national debt stood at 115% of GDP last year against the EU's 60% reference, and the country is under the Excessive Deficit Procedure ahead of the May 2027 presidential election. Two asset managers quoted took a pessimistic view, with Ninety One's John Stopford saying he expects France is heading towards a crisis, though that is a forecast rather than a market consensus. In India, the benchmark 2036 bond ended at 6.9452%, its highest close since early June — reports give the comparison date as either 8 or 11 June — after an 11 basis-point rise across August, the largest monthly increase of the financial year.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Sovereign yields set the reference rate for corporate borrowing, so a simultaneous move in three large markets raises the cost of capital for customers and suppliers at the same time. The construction and property end-markets that are meaningful consumers of adhesive technologies are among the most sensitive to that, and the effect arrives with a lag. The French case is worth separating from the others: it reflects fiscal and political risk rather than the energy shock, which means it may not unwind if oil retreats. Points that may be worth considering include how project pipelines with 2027 financing dates are stress-tested against a higher rate path, and whether the divergence between energy-driven and fiscally-driven yield moves changes how country risk is weighted in European planning.

The Economic Times | Cnyes | Commercial Times | The Economic Times | MarketScreener | Channel News Asia | Commercial Times | Business Recorder

item.title: The US and Iran attacked each other for the first time in about a month, lifting oil more than 2% and Brent back to about USD 90, and Trump said Kharg Island was being "blown to smithereens" in a post carrying an AI-generated video.
item.description:
The exchange broke a lull of roughly a month. A US attack on rocket launchers on Iran's Larak island, about 660 kilometres east of Kharg, was followed by an Iranian assault on two US bases in Jordan. Oil rose more than 2% and Brent returned to about USD 90 a barrel. Trump's one-line social-media post claiming that Kharg Island was being destroyed was accompanied by an AI-generated video clip, and no other evidence emerged that the facility was under attack; Vice President JD Vance said afterwards that the post was intended as a message to Tehran. The distinction matters commercially, because Kharg handled about 90% of Iran's oil exports before the war began on 28 February, so real damage there would be a different event from a rhetorical one. Equity markets were mixed to lower, with the Dow down almost 0.5% at the open. Two adjustments already under way continued: Asian refiners in China, South Korea and Japan increased purchases of Argentine crude, with Japan's Eneos Holdings and Taiyo Oil buying Medanito grade for the first time, and Bloomberg has documented an LPG cargo that reached India from the US in June after 48 days at sea, roughly seven times the usual Gulf voyage and, Bloomberg estimates, possibly 30% more in freight. Trump was due to meet oil refining executives on Tuesday to discuss increasing refining capacity. Separately, the Centre for Economics and Business Research estimated the war will reduce UK real disposable income by GBP 70.4 billion, about GBP 2,400 per household over two years.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Energy and freight are the two channels that reach adhesive technologies production most directly, and both moved in the same direction. Crude near USD 90 feeds through to naphtha and to the petrochemical derivatives that sit upstream of adhesive technologies, and it raises the cost of the packaging materials many customers buy. The rerouting evidence is arguably the more durable signal: an LPG voyage taking seven times as long at a possible 30% freight premium, and Japanese refiners qualifying an Argentine grade for the first time alongside increased Chinese and South Korean buying, describe sourcing decisions being remade rather than temporarily disrupted. Points that may be worth considering include how far current formulation and sourcing assumptions still rest on pre-war freight economics, and how a claim of the Kharg type — unverified, but market-moving — should be handled in commercial planning.

Asharq Al-Awsat | Asharq Al-Awsat | The Times of India | The Economic Times | Cnyes | Lianhe Zaobao | Bloomberg | South China Morning Post | The Independent
